questions.q: Identify the official designation of the character who first orders the tree to be cut in the story.
questions.a: Correct Answer: The District Magistrate (जिलाधिकारी / कलेक्टर) orders the tree to be cut initially. A wrong answer (e.g., "the engineer" or "the mother") reveals the student cannot distinguish between the issuing authority and the executing agents, indicating weak literal retrieval of hierarchical roles in the narrative.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the old man (नछ गकवक वकनेह) refuses to leave the tree even when threatened with death.
questions.a: Correct Answer: The old man identifies himself as a poet whose life's work (songs, poems) is inseparable from the tree; the tree is the physical anchor of his creative identity and the village's collective memory. A wrong answer focusing only on "stubbornness" or "fear of death" shows the student treats the character as a flat plot device rather than inferring the symbolic fusion of artist, art, and habitat.

questions.q: The mother (एकी) says: "वपंक गकवक रुक एगक्जस औवक्जर िज फजक, वक्सज देज िज फजरक रक्स झ<+ ध गह ववव तकरह।" What literal danger does she describe, and what inferential warning about the tree's roots does she imply?
questions.a: Correct Answer: Literal: If the tree falls on the road, a big accident will occur. Inferential: The tree's roots have spread under the road, so cutting it destabilizes the road itself—nature and infrastructure are entangled. A wrong answer that only states the literal danger misses the ecological/structural inference, showing inability to read spatial causality in the text.

questions.q: Compare the responses of the Engineer (इककफजावसामसाव) and the District Magistrate (जिलाधिकारी) when they learn the tree was planted by a former ruler. What does this contrast reveal about their respective relationships to authority?
questions.a: Correct Answer: The Engineer immediately halts work citing departmental jurisdiction, showing rigid procedural compliance. The Magistrate investigates and transfers the decision to the Forest Department, revealing political pragmatism. The contrast infers that bureaucracy follows rules, while administration negotiates power—both fail to value the tree intrinsically.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The story portrays the government machinery as entirely heartless." Defend your judgment using two specific textual episodes.
questions.a: Correct Answer: The statement is partially false. Episode 1: The Magistrate *does* halt cutting when historical significance emerges, showing procedural humanity. Episode 2: The Forest Department officer saves the tree by invoking a higher ecological law. The machinery is rigid, not heartless—it responds to legal/historical frameworks, not emotional appeals. A student calling it wholly heartless fails to evaluate nuance in institutional behavior.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from the perspective of the tamarind tree on the night before the Forest Officer arrives, blending literal sensory details from the text with an inferred emotional voice.
questions.a: Expected criteria: Must include (a) literal detail: "roots under the road," "birds' nests," "poet's songs"; (b) inferred voice: ancient witness, quiet resilience, fear of saws. Poor answer: generic "I am scared" without textual anchors. Good answer: "Tonight my roots tremble under the asphalt; the poet's verses rustle in my leaves like prayers. The saws paused today—will the green seal hold?"
